threads_text: Undergrad computer science enrollment at four-year colleges just fell 12.4% in one year, new National Student Clearinghouse data shows. Over two years, graduate CS has lost 27.1% of its students as AI squeezes entry-level coding jobs. Would you still tell a kid to major in computer science?

paragraphs.text: Undergraduate enrollment in computer science at US four-year colleges fell 12.4% from a year earlier this fall, according to preliminary data from the National Student Clearinghouse Research Center reported on October 29, 2026. Higher Ed Dive said computer science saw the biggest losses of any subject area in the data.

Graduate enrollment in computer and information sciences fell more than 10% this fall, Bloomberg reported. At two-year colleges, computer and information sciences enrollment fell 12.3%, after a 5.9% drop the previous fall, according to Community College Daily.

The decline is now in its second year. Over two years, undergraduate computer science enrollment has fallen 18.4% at four-year institutions and 17.5% at two-year colleges, while graduate computer science enrollment has fallen 27.1%, Community College Daily reported. Bloomberg noted that this year's drop follows a decline last year that ended years of growth.
That growth had been steep. National Science Foundation figures cited by The Next Web show that computer science bachelor's degrees rose from about 56,000 in 2014 to about 122,000 in 2024.

Matthew Holsapple, senior director of research at the Clearinghouse, called the figures "just remarkable declines," according to Bloomberg. He said students are finding paths that suit them beyond the traditional route, and that affordability is almost certainly one factor.

Bloomberg linked the decline to artificial intelligence, reporting that AI has made it harder for computer science graduates to find jobs as companies eliminate many entry-level coding roles. The outlet also cited an August report from the Bureau of Labor Statistics that found computer and mathematics jobs would feel the most impact from AI of any occupational group.

Researchers have pointed to other possible causes as well. The Next Web, describing an earlier study of college course enrollment by Stanford economist Jacob Light, reported that he did not attribute the decline to AI and listed several possible drivers, including a weaker market for junior developers, doubts about the value of the degree and the rise of data science.

Overall undergraduate enrollment still rose 0.6% this fall, slower than the 2.4% growth of fall 2025, Higher Ed Dive reported. Undergraduate enrollment in engineering and in health professions each rose more than 6%. Graduate enrollment fell 1.6% overall, and master's enrollment fell 3.7%. The preliminary data covers 46% of reporting institutions, and final fall figures are due in January.

In NeuraFeed's reading, the numbers suggest students are reacting quickly to signals from the job market. Engineering and health programs are growing while computer science shrinks, which points to a shift in where students see stable careers rather than a retreat from technical study as a whole.
Watch the final Clearinghouse figures in January, which will show whether the preliminary 12.4% drop holds once all reporting institutions are counted.
